summary: Before a huge crowd, Jesus warns His disciples against hypocrisy and greed, tells of a rich fool, and calls them to fear God and trust their Father.
key_insight: Hypocrisy and greed look like different sins, but Jesus answers both with the same words: “Do not fear.” Hypocrisy fears what people will think; greed fears not having enough. The answer to both is the Father who numbers every hair and is pleased “to give you the kingdom.”
story: Meanwhile a crowd of many thousands had gathered, so many that they trampled one another. Jesus spoke first to His disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Nothing covered would stay hidden, and what they whispered in inner rooms would be proclaimed on the housetops.

“And I say to you, My friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do.” They were to fear God, who has power to cast into hell. Yet that same God does not forget a single sparrow, though five are sold for two copper coins. “But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.”

Whoever confessed Him before men, the Son of Man would confess before the angels of God; whoever denied Him would be denied. A word against the Son of Man could be forgiven, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. And when they were brought before synagogues and rulers, they need not worry what to say, “For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.”

Then someone in the crowd called out, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Jesus answered, “Man, who made Me a judge or an arbitrator over you?” And He said to them all, “Take heed and beware of covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses.”

He told them a parable. A rich man’s land produced so much that he had no room for his crops. So he decided to pull down his barns and build bigger ones, and then say to himself, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; take your ease; eat, drink, and be merry.” But God said to him, “Fool! This night your soul will be required of you; then whose will those things be which you have provided?” “So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”

To His disciples He said, “Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat; nor about the body, what you will put on.” The ravens neither sow nor reap and have no barn, yet God feeds them; the lilies neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon was never dressed like them. The nations chase after food and drink, but “your Father knows that you need these things.” “But seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.”

“Do not fear, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” So they should sell what they had and give alms, storing up treasure in heaven, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

scene.label: Five sparrows
scene.text: Sparrows were the cheapest birds in the market, food for the poor. Matthew records two sold for a copper coin (Matthew 10:29); here five go for two coins, as if the fifth were thrown in for nothing. Even that extra bird is not forgotten before God.

scene.label: Dividing an inheritance
scene.text: People often asked a respected teacher to settle family disputes. Under the Law the firstborn received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17). Jesus’ reply echoes the question once thrown at Moses: “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14).

scene.label: Eat, drink and be merry
scene.text: The rich man’s plan echoes a familiar saying (Ecclesiastes 8:15). In Isaiah the people of Jerusalem added, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” (Isaiah 22:13). The rich man counted on many years; God told him it would be tonight.

scene.label: Ravens
scene.text: Matthew says “birds of the air” (Matthew 6:26); Luke names ravens, birds the Law counted unclean (Leviticus 11:15). Scripture says God feeds even them (Job 38:41; Psalm 147:9). If God provides for an unclean scavenger, He will not forget His children.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records the man with the inheritance and the parable of the rich fool, and both fit his steady warnings about wealth (6:24; 16:19–31). Matthew records many of the other sayings in other settings (Matthew 10:26–33; 6:25–33); Jesus likely repeated His teaching as He traveled, and Luke gathers it here under one theme. Luke alone adds the tender “little flock” and the Father’s good pleasure to give them the kingdom.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Son of Man who will confess or deny people before the angels of God. He also speaks as the Son who knows the Father’s care down to a sparrow and a single hair, and He gives that confidence to His little flock.
seeing.living: Ask whether fear of people is shaping what you say about Jesus, and whether fear of having too little is shaping what you keep. The rich man planned for many years and never planned for God. Being rich toward God means trusting the Father enough to give.
seeing.ponder: If God said to you, “This night,” whose would your things be, and what would you wish you had given?

preaching.big_idea: Fear God and trust your Father, and hypocrisy and greed lose their hold.
outline: Trust the Father, not your barns (22–31)
preaching.watch_for: The rich fool talks only to himself (v. 17) and to his own soul (v. 19): “my crops,” “my barns,” “my goods.” The first other voice in the story is God’s, and His first word is “Fool!” (v. 20).
